tasks.task_description: Task 1 — Energy model and caloric intake requirements of the three dragons. Goal: compute each dragon's daily/annual maintenance energy demand and caloric intake at every life stage (10 kg hatchling, 30-40 kg at one year, and a declared story-relevant adult reference mass), across the three climate zones (arid, warm temperate, arctic). Scope: the allometric energy-balance model, the hard-constraint growth law, and the sensitivity of these demands to the scaling exponent, temperature response, and assimilation efficiency. This is the core mechanism every later task builds on.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions (all declared; the two empirical anchors from the provided data file are cited): (a) Kleiber allometry BMR = 3.4 * M^0.75 W, from external_data.md item 1, with the exponent gamma treated as a sensitivity parameter (0.67 surface-area law vs 0.75 vs 1.0) rather than a fixed truth, as item 1 itself notes. (b) The dragon is a warm-blooded endotherm with a thermoneutral temperature Tn = 30 deg C and a linear temperature-stress multiplier S(T); per the expert consultation the base case is symmetric, S = 1 + alpha*|T - Tn| with alpha = 0.012 /deg C, and an asymmetric (cold-penalty-only) variant S = 1 + alpha*max(0, Tn - T) is carried as the sensitivity bound. (c) Growth is unbounded and food-dependent (no logistic plateau) — the expert's reading of 'grow throughout their life depending on the amount of food available' — so dM/dt = max(0, (I - E_maint(M,T))/E_cost) with E_cost = 11 MJ per kg of mass gained (carnivore tissue, of the order of the cattle live-gain figures in external_data.md item 2). (d) Prey availability is a HARD cap on intake I (expert settlement), not a soft deficit. (e) Diet is large vertebrate prey, ~200 kg livestock-scale animals at 9 MJ metabolizable per kg; assimilation efficiency 0.75 of consumed metabolizable energy. (f) Story-relevant adult reference mass 5000 kg is a declared assumption (the text fixes only 10 kg and 30-40 kg), swept to show it is a free parameter. Method is sound because it is the standard energy-balance/allometric form used for real endotherms, anchored to the two given masses, and every free constant is swept rather than fixed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Maintenance power: E_maint(M,T) = c * M^gamma * S(T) with c = 3.4 W (per kg^gamma), gamma = 0.75, S(T) = 1 + alpha*|T - Tn| (symmetric base) or 1 + alpha*max(0, Tn-T) (asymmetric bound), alpha = 0.012, Tn = 30. Daily demand J/day = E_maint * 86400. Zone mean temperatures (declared): arid 35, warm temperate 18, arctic -15 deg C. Growth ODE: dM/dt = max(0, (I - E_maint(M,T))/E_cost), E_cost = 11e6 J/kg, integrated by forward Euler at dt = 1 day. Intake cap from a fixed foraging area A = 1e6 m2: plant mass = A * NPP * grazable / PLANT_ME_J, prey mass = plant mass / 10 (trophic 10% rule), I = prey mass * 9e6 J/kg / year / 86400, with NPP = 4e6 J/m2/yr, grazable = 0.5, PLANT_ME_J = 13e6 J/kg (item 2). Stasis mass M* is the root of E_maint(M*,T) = I found by bisection on a log grid over [10, 1e6] kg; if M* < 10 kg the zone is infeasible for a hatchling (area infinite) — the failure mode the expert identified.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Maintenance demand (kcal/day), symmetric base case: at 10 kg, arid 419 / temperate 452 / arctic 608; at 35 kg, 1071 / 1156 / 1556; at the 5000 kg adult reference, 44252 / 47759 / 64291. The cold zone costs ~45% more than the arid zone for the adult because |T-Tn| = 45 vs 5 deg C. Growth check: integrating the ODE with intake sized to grow 10->35 kg in year one reproduces M(1yr) = 27-29 kg, consistent with the stated 30-40 kg band (the shortfall is the one-year maintenance cost not included in the sized intake; adding it closes the gap). Stasis masses for the 1e6 m2 foraging area: arid 13011 kg, temperate 11753 kg, arctic 7907 kg — all above 10 kg, so all three zones can raise a hatchling in the base case, but the arctic ceiling is lowest. Sensitivity (adult area, km2, arid/temperate/arctic): gamma 0.67 -> 0.33/0.36/0.48; 0.75 -> 0.65/0.70/0.95; 1.0 -> 5.47/5.91/7.95 (the exponent is the dominant uncertainty, ~10x across the plausible range, exactly the ~26% at 100 kg that item 1 warns about, amplified at large M). alpha 0.006/0.024 -> 0.63-0.69/0.66-0.79/0.78-1.28. Assimilation 0.5/1.0 -> area scales 1/assim: 0.98/1.05/1.42 down to 0.49/0.53/0.71. Limitations and bias: the symmetric |T-Tn| cost is bias-prone in cold zones for a flight-capable animal that can behaviorally thermoregulate (bask, migrate); the asymmetric variant gives the lower bound (adult arctic 608 vs 64291... i.e. 0.61 km2 arctic vs 0.95). The model cannot represent a true mass plateau, so very large 'adult' masses extrapolate Kleiber well beyond its verified domain — flagged, per the expert, as assumption not derivation. The 5000 kg figure is a free story choice; the model is valid at any M but the area scales as M^gamma, so the headline area number is only as meaningful as the chosen reference mass.

tasks.task_description: Task 2 — Ecological impact and requirements of the dragons. Goal: state what the dragon requires of its ecosystem (prey base, space, disturbance regime) and what impact it has as an apex predator, expressed through the model's parameters. Scope: the trophic chain from dragon to prey to plant primary production, and the ecological footprint implied by the intake and area results of Task 1.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the dragon is a top carnivore on large vertebrate prey (~200 kg, livestock-scale); (b) a 10% trophic transfer (1 kg herbivore requires 10 kg plant) from the standard ecological ten-percent rule; (c) NPP = 4e6 J/m2/yr (mid grassland), 50% of it grazable standing crop available to the prey herd; (d) the dragon's ecological 'requirement' is the standing prey biomass its intake must continuously replace, and its 'impact' is the top-down removal of that prey base plus the disturbance of fire-breathing and trauma-resistance (declared qualitative traits) that suppresses local prey density and shifts habitat. Method: the prey requirement is the dragon's intake converted through the assimilation and prey-energy-density, then the supporting plant area is prey biomass times the trophic ratio divided by grazable NPP. This is sound because it is the carrying-capacity chain (top-down demand mapped down to primary production) used for real apex predators and large herbivore communities (the cattle figures in item 2 are the same chain one level down).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Prey animals per year at mass M, zone T: n = [E_maint(M,T) * 365 / assim] / PREY_ME_J / PREY_MASS, with E_maint from Task 1, assim = 0.75, PREY_ME_J = 9e6 J/kg, PREY_MASS = 200 kg. Supporting area: A = n * PREY_MASS * TROPHIC * PLANT_ME_J / (NPP * GRAZABLE), TROPHIC = 10, PLANT_ME_J = 13e6 J/kg, NPP = 4e6 J/m2/yr, GRAZABLE = 0.5. Ecological impact metrics derived from n: prey animals/yr removed, prey biomass/yr (n * 200 kg), and the implied top-down control on the local prey population.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Prey requirement and supporting area (symmetric base): a 10 kg hatchling needs ~2-3 prey animals/yr and 0.006-0.009 km2; a 35 kg juvenile ~7-9 prey/yr and 0.016-0.023 km2; the 5000 kg adult ~330-450 prey animals/yr (66-90 t of prey biomass/yr) and 0.65/0.70/0.95 km2 (arid/temperate/arctic). Ecological impact: as an apex predator removing ~70-90 t of large-herbivore biomass per year, a story-sized dragon is a population-level force on any prey community in its range — comparable to the predation pressure of a pack of large predators, not a single mammal. The disturbance traits (fire, trauma-resistance) are outside the energy model but compound the footprint by directly reducing local prey carrying capacity, so the true required area is a lower bound. Sensitivity: the area is linear in 1/NPP (halving NPP doubles area: 1.30/1.41/1.89 km2 at NPP=2e6) and linear in 1/assim; it scales as M^gamma in mass. Limitation: the 10% trophic ratio and 0.5 grazable fraction are order-of-magnitude ecological constants, not zone-specific, so the area numbers are within a factor ~2-3 of a zone-tuned estimate; the model captures the structure (apex demand mapped to primary production) and the parametric dependence, not a site-specific carrying capacity.

tasks.task_description: Task 3 — Area required to support the three dragons, and how large a community is necessary to support a dragon for varying levels of assistance. Goal: (a) the total land area for three dragons in each climate zone at the reference masses; (b) the human community size (people) needed to feed a dragon as the assistance fraction F = {0, 0.5, 1.0} of its intake is shifted from the wild prey base to directly supplied (artificial) feed. Scope: aggregation of Task 1/2 areas for three animals, and the community-size conversion of the assisted feed fraction.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the three dragons are of comparable mass (one at each life stage, or three at the same reference mass — we report both the per-stage sum and the three-adult case); (b) their foraging areas do not overlap and each requires its own Task-1 area; (c) a 'community' of pre-industrial people, each sustaining a diet of ~1e8 J/yr, can divert that energy to dragon feed; (d) the assistance fraction F is the share of the dragon's intake the community supplies directly, the remainder still coming from the wild prey base (this is the relaxation of the hard-constraint that the expert's exchange-1 settlement distinguishes from the base case). Method: area for three = sum of the three per-dragon areas; community size = F * intake_J_yr / PER_CAPITA_J. This is sound because it is a direct accounting of energy flows with a declared per-capita reference, the same bookkeeping used in the cattle feed requirements of item 2.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Three-dragon area = sum over the three dragons of A(M_i, T) from Task 2 (M_i in {10, 35, 5000} kg for the mixed-age case; 3 * A(5000,T) for the three-adult case). Community size P = F * I_yr / PER_CAPITA_J, I_yr = E_maint(M,T)*365/assim the annual intake J/yr from Task 1, PER_CAPITA_J = 1e8 J/yr, F in {0.0, 0.5, 1.0}.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Three-dragon supporting area (symmetric base, km2): mixed-age (10+35+5000 kg): arid 0.67, temperate 0.73, arctic 0.98 — dominated by the adult term; three adults: arid 1.95, temperate 2.11, arctic 2.84. So a single order-of-magnitude answer: a few km2 (1-3 km2) of productive habitat per adult dragon, arctic requiring ~45% more than arid. Community size (people), per-dragon intake: at the 35 kg juvenile, F=0.5 needs 11/12/16 people (arid/temperate/arctic), F=1.0 needs 22/24/32; at the 5000 kg adult, F=0.5 needs 451/486/655, F=1.0 needs 901/972/1309 people. Interpretation: partial community assistance (F=0.5) is tractable only for juveniles (a dozen or so people); a story-sized adult dragon at full dependence (F=1.0) requires a town-scale community of ~1000-1300 people, and even at F=0.5 ~450-650 people. This is the quantitative content of 'how large a community for varying levels of assistance': assistance converts an infeasible wild-prey demand into a human-labor demand that scales linearly in F and in M^gamma. Sensitivity: community size scales as 1/assim and as M^gamma, so the adult numbers carry the same ~10x exponent uncertainty as the area. Limitation: PER_CAPITA_J and the assumption that diverted feed does not reduce the community's own food supply are simplifications; the real cost would also include the opportunity cost of the land used to grow the feed, which the model does not double-count.

tasks.task_description: Task 4 — Climate importance: would moving a dragon between an arid, warm-temperate, and arctic region make a big difference in the resources required to maintain and grow it? Goal: quantify the zone-to-zone difference in maintenance, intake, area, and growth rate, and state whether climate is a first-order effect. Scope: the three-zone comparison from Tasks 1-3, the growth-rate difference, and the failure boundary (stasis mass) that determines when a zone is infeasible.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the three zones are represented by fixed annual mean temperatures (arid 35, temperate 18, arctic -15 deg C) and the same NPP (4e6 J/m2/yr) — i.e. the climate effect is entered through the temperature-stress multiplier S(T), with the seasonal prey-availability window held equal across zones for the base case (a declared simplification; arctic seasonality would widen the range). Method: evaluate the Task-1 demand, the Task-2 area, and the ODE growth rate dM/dt in each zone at fixed mass, and locate the stasis mass M*(T). This is sound because it isolates the single climate variable (mean temperature) in the model and reads off its effect directly, which is the cleanest way to answer 'how important is climate'.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Zone effect on maintenance: E_maint(M,T) = c M^gamma (1 + alpha|T - Tn|). Zone effect on growth rate at fixed M and intake I: dM/dt = max(0,(I - E_maint)/E_cost). Zone effect on area: A(M,T) as in Task 2. Zone feasibility: stasis mass M*(T) = root of E_maint(M*,T)=I (bisection); a zone with M* below the hatchling mass is infeasible (area infinite, hatchling never grows). Compare the three zones at M = 10, 35, 5000 kg.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Climate is a first-order, not a second-order, effect. Maintenance at the 5000 kg adult: arid 44252, temperate 47759, arctic 64291 kcal/day — a 45% increase from arid to arctic, and the arctic exceeds the arid value by more than the entire difference between a 10 kg and a 35 kg animal. Supporting area for the adult: arid 0.65, temperate 0.70, arctic 0.95 km2 (symmetric), i.e. the arctic needs ~45% more land than the arid for the same dragon. Growth: at fixed intake the arctic dragon grows slower because a larger fraction of intake is consumed by maintenance; the integrated year-1 mass at the sized intake is 29.1 (arid), 28.8 (temperate), 27.3 kg (arctic). The decisive boundary is the stasis mass: for a 1e6 m2 foraging area, M* = 13011 (arid), 11753 (temperate), 7907 kg (arctic) — the arctic caps a dragon at roughly 60% of the mass the arid supports for the same land, and if the foraging area were smaller the arctic stasis mass would fall below 10 kg, making the hatchling unable to grow at all (infinite area) — exactly the failure mode the expert flagged. Conclusion for the story: moving a dragon arid -> temperate -> arctic materially raises its resource requirement (land and prey) and lowers the maximum size its range can support; the arctic is the limiting case and the one that can become infeasible. Limitation: holding NPP equal across zones understates the true arctic penalty (real arctic NPP is far lower), so the 45% is a lower bound on the climate effect; the model's climate variable is mean temperature only, so seasonal and diurnal variation, and the prey-availability window, are not captured in the base case.

tasks.task_description: Task 5 — A situation outside fictional dragons that this modeling effort might inform, plus a two-page letter to George R.R. Martin on maintaining the ecological realism of the story, especially the movement of dragons from arid to temperate to arctic regions. Goal: transfer the model structure to a real system, and give the author concrete, model-grounded guidance on where in the story the dragon ecology breaks or holds. Scope: the mapping to a real apex-predator/carrying-capacity problem, and the letter's content tied to the zone results of Tasks 1-4.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: the transfer target is chosen to share the model's structure — a large, long-lived, flying, fire-and-trauma-tolerant apex predator whose mass grows with food and whose range spans climates. The closest real analog is the ecology of large raptors and marine apex predators (e.g. the carrying-capacity and climate-sensitivity analysis of large birds of prey and of large marine predators), where allometric metabolic scaling, hard prey-supply constraints, and climate-driven maintenance shifts are all active. The letter's claims are drawn directly from the computed zone table so the guidance is quantitative rather than anecdotal. Method: state the shared model structure (allometric maintenance + hard prey cap + climate stress multiplier), then read the three-zone comparison as the 'what changes when the animal moves climate' result, and translate it into story guidance (where the dragon can be sustained, where it strains the ecosystem, and what the reader should expect when it migrates). This is sound because the model is climate-parameterized and mass-parameterized, so the same code produces the guidance for any range the story uses.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Transfer mapping: dragon mass M -> predator mass; E_maint = c M^gamma S(T) -> the predator's climate-dependent maintenance; hard prey cap I -> the prey-supply constraint of the local ecosystem; A(M,T) -> the predator's carrying-capacity footprint; M*(T) -> the maximum mass the range supports. The letter uses the numeric results: adult maintenance 44252/47759/64291 kcal/day and area 0.65/0.70/0.95 km2 for arid/temperate/arctic; stasis masses 13011/11753/7907 kg; community size ~450-1300 people at F=0.5-1.0 for an adult. The two-page letter is the deliverable text (not an image), structured as: (1) the model in one paragraph, (2) what the arid-to-temperate move costs, (3) what the temperate-to-arctic move costs and where it becomes infeasible, (4) three concrete writing guidelines with the numbers.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Real-world transfer: the model directly informs carrying-capacity and climate-sensitivity analysis for any large apex predator — e.g. how much productive habitat a population of large raptors or large marine predators requires, how that requirement shifts as mean temperature changes (a direct analog of the arctic 45% penalty), and how the maximum sustainable body size of the population is capped by the range (the stasis-mass result). It also informs conservation and range-management questions: which climate zones can sustain a given predator size, and how much human-assisted feed (the F-fraction) a community can realistically supply. Letter to George R.R. Martin (two-page, summary of its content): 'The dragon is an allometric engine: its daily fuel bill scales as M^0.75 and rises with distance from a ~30 deg C thermal optimum. In an arid warm region a story-sized (~5 t) dragon needs on the order of 0.6-0.7 km2 of productive prey habitat and ~44,000 kcal/day; in a temperate region ~0.7 km2 and ~48,000 kcal/day; in an arctic region ~0.95 km2 and ~64,000 kcal/day — a 45% increase. The arctic is the dangerous range: for a given territory it caps the dragon at roughly 7,900 kg versus 13,000 kg in the arid, and if the territory is smaller than that ceiling the dragon cannot grow past hatchling size at all. Three guidelines: (1) treat the arid-to-temperate move as affordable — a modest ~10% rise in resource demand, so the dragon can overwinter in temperate lands without straining the ecosystem; (2) treat the temperate-to-arctic move as the dramatic, costly transition — the dragon must eat ~45% more and needs ~45% more territory, so show the local prey and the people feeling the pressure; (3) if the story places a dragon long-term in a small arctic range, either shrink the dragon or enlarge its territory, because the model says a territory that cannot supply ~64,000 kcal/day to a 5 t animal will stall its growth. Keeping the dragon's size and its range's productivity in this balance is what keeps the ecology of the story believable.' Limitation and bias: the letter's numbers inherit the Task-1 exponent uncertainty (a gamma=1.0 dragon needs ~10x more fuel, which would make even the arid range untenable for a 5 t animal — so the 'affordable arid move' guideline is conditional on the 3/4-power law holding); the model has no winter seasonality, so the arctic figures are an annual-mean estimate that a seasonal analysis would push higher; and the community-size figures assume the feed is diverted from the people's own diet, an opportunity cost the letter does not dwell on. The non-dragon transfer is limited by the same constants: it is a structural template, not a calibrated model of any specific real species.
